title: POC SLO & Sampling Proposal TTFT vs TPOT - SkyBridge
summary: Scoping call to align on POC success criteria focusing on latency SLOs (first-token TTFT and total-token TPOT), sampling plan, measurement methodology, and timeline. Discussed target p95/p99 thresholds, payload variance, traffic stitching approach, benchmark harness, and next steps for a 3-week pilot. Some transcript artifacts and name mis-hearings present.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-08-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Ortiz (Redwood Solutions), Samir Patel (SkyBridge CTO), Elena Marks (SkyBridge Head of ML), Rajiv Kapoor (SkyBridge SRE), Maya Chen (Product)

Auto-generated Summary (may be rough): Align on SLOs (TTFT & TPOT), sampling windows, runbook for benchmarks, send benchmark harness + security pack, schedule pilot start next Tuesday.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh, quick round-robin — Priya, Samir O, we'll jump into the SLO design and then lock down what you need for the pilot.
[00:12] Samir Patel: Thanks. we've got — sorry, been pulled between meetings — but we really want to be clear on what success looks like. We're trying to choose between an emphasis on first token latency versus total response latency, and cost tradeoffs matter.
[00:25] Priya Nair: Yep. And just to set expectations, Redwood typically measures both TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TPOT (time-to-last-token / total per-request). For chat workloads with streaming we often prioritize TTFT p95/p99, but for batch generation or longer outputs TPOT p95 matters more.
[00:45] Rajiv Kapoor: Can you clarify p95 vs p99 targets? like, what's realistic on H100 vs A100?
[00:52] Priya Nair: Sure. For a 2k-token average response, on H100 dedicated configs we see TTFT p95 ~ 120-160ms and p99 ~ 220-350ms for common open models when batching is tuned. TPOT is much wider — p95 might be 1.8-2.5s and p99 3.5-6s depending on decoding settings and kv cache hits. those are ballpark numbers.
[01:20] Elena Marks: Our typical payloads vary — some short responses (60-120 tokens) for assistant prompts, and some long syntheses (~2k tokens) for daily reports. So the distribution is bimodal. We need SLOs that reflect both.
[01:38] Jordan Lee: Great note. For a POC we recommend defining two SLO buckets: interactive (<= 250 tokens) with tight TTFT and delivery targets, and long-run generation (>= 1000 tokens) with relaxed TTFT but TPOT monitoring.
[01:52] Maya Chen: What's the recommended p95/p99 for interactive? we need to give stakeholders numbers.
[01:58] Priya Nair: Recommend interactive TTFT p95 = 200ms, p99 = 350ms. TPOT p95 = 650ms, p99 = 1.2s for <=250 tokens. For long runs, TTFT p95 = 350ms, p99 = 600ms, TPOT p95 = 3s, p99 = 6s. Those are starting points; we'll calibrate during the benchmark.
[02:26] Samir Patel: Ok that makes sense. how do you measure TTFT for streaming vs non-streaming? we use streaming in prod.
[02:33] Priya Nair: For streaming, TTFT is measured as the timestamp when the first byte/chunk arrives to the client. For non-streaming, it's the time until the first token output by the model. we instrument end-to-end from Redwood SDK or your client to capture network time. we also recommend synthetic clients inside your VPC to measure network-local latencies.
[02:56] Jordan Lee: One wrinkle is caching: prefix/KV cache dramatically changes TPOT for multi-turn chat. We should model both cold-cache and warm-cache traffic during the run.
[03:08] Rajiv Kapoor: How do you simulate a warm cache?
[03:11] Priya Nair: Warm-cache scenario is a pre-warm phase — we replay representative prefix sequences to populate KV caches before load sweeps. We'll include warm and cold runs in the plan.
[03:21] Samir Patel: On sample size — what's needed to confidently say p99 improved or regressed? we have limited time.
[03:28] Priya Nair: For p99 estimation with decent confidence, we usually need thousands of samples per bucket. A heuristic: 10k samples gives stable p99 estimates across noise. For a 3-week POC we can concentrate traffic across representative windows — e.g., 3 independent runs of 3k-5k requests per traffic profile.
[03:52] Elena Marks: That seems heavy. can we do stratified sampling? like focus on more frequent user shapes?
[03:58] Priya Nair: Absolutely. We typically stratify by payload size and by turn depth. So you'll get more samples from interactive short-turn traffic and fewer from long synths, but still ensure minimal sample counts for p99 stability.
[04:10] Jordan Lee: Let's talk measurement methodology — Redwood will provide a benchmark harness (link: https://redwood.example/bench-harness) that runs in your env. It can instrument requests, collect per-token timestamps, and export to Prometheus or our CSV. We'll need a golden prompt-set and traffic profile from you.
[04:28] Maya Chen: We have a prompt corpus (internal doc link), can share sanitized subset. Also we need to verify compliance on logs shipped out.
[04:35] Jordan Lee: We'll run the harness within your VPC. By default we don't pull logs out; we can push aggregated metrics only. For security pack we'll share SOC2 artifact links and an SSO integration doc.
[04:48] Rajiv Kapoor: Regarding measurement windows — during a load test do you recommend steady-state windows or ramp-and-hold?
[04:54] Priya Nair: Ramp-and-hold with multiple steady-state windows is best. Typical cadence: cold-start baseline, 5-10 minute ramp to target QPS, 10-15 minute steady-state, then cool down. Repeat for 3-5 target points and also run a spike profile. We'll capture TTFT/TPOT distributions during steady-state.
[05:12] Samir Patel: QPS targets — we want to validate both 200 req/s and burst to 800 for peak events. Is that feasible?
[05:18] Priya Nair: Yes, we'll size the Dedicated pool for those throughput points. We'll also run an autoscaling stress scenario to test fallbacks. Note cost tradeoffs: higher burst headroom increases reserved capacity needs.
[05:30] Elena Marks: How do you handle decoding variance (top-k vs sampling), temperature?
[05:33] Priya Nair: We'll fix decoding settings for benchmarks that mirror prod: top-p 0.95, temperature 0.2 for deterministic tasks, and a separate sampling profile for creative generation. Decoding impacts throughput, so we log model config with each run.
[05:47] Jordan Lee: On acceptance criteria for the POC — proposed: 1) TTFT/TPOT p95/p99 thresholds met for the interactive bucket across 3 independent steady-state runs; 2) No more than 2% error budget for 99th percentile latency breaches during steady-state; 3) Throughput validated at target QPS with <5% request loss or timeouts.
[06:08] Samir Patel: That error budget item — can we define it as percent of requests exceeding p99? or percent of steady-state time above threshold?
[06:15] Priya Nair: We'll define both: primary metric percent of requests above p99 (should be <= 2% across runs) and secondary metric percent of time where rolling p95 exceeds threshold (should be <= 1% ideally). we'll document exact formulas in the measurement plan.
[06:32] Rajiv Kapoor: Who owns instrumentation? We want everything reproducible.
[06:36] Jordan Lee: Redwood provides the harness and test runner. SkyBridge will provide the prompt corpus and a VPC sandbox. SREs will run the harness and collect logs. Redwood SE will help interpret results.
[06:46] Maya Chen: Timeline? can we kick tomorrow?
[06:48] Jordan Lee: Practically we need two business days to provision the harness and share network ACL checklist. Ideal pilot start Monday next week (2027-08-31). Given today is the 30th, that's tight but doable if SkyBridge can provision the sandbox today.
[07:00] Samir Patel: We'll prioritize — Rajiv will open a ticket and get creds to you.
[07:04] Rajiv Kapoor: I'll create the sandbox and share the IAM roles. ETA end of day.
[07:08] Priya Nair: Great. Now some measurement nitpicks — we should also capture percentile confidence intervals. Redwood will compute bootstrap CI for p95/p99 and include in the report so you can see statistical significance between runs.
[07:23] Elena Marks: Sounds good. for comparison we'll run a baseline on existing infra and then run Redwood Dedicated.
[07:29] Jordan Lee: We'll help script that comparison. One more operational point: We'll also instrument model variant fallbacks (e.g., quantized fp16 vs int8) and log quality deltas. If quality drop is unacceptable, we'll flag in the report.
[07:43] Maya Chen: How do you capture quality? we have subjective evals and automated metrics.
[07:47] Priya Nair: For POC we'll use a mix: ROUGE/BLEU-ish for synthesis and a small human eval for 100 sample prompts. We'll correlate quality with latency buckets.
[07:58] Jordan Lee: Okay real transcript snippet — some words may be a little garbled in the auto transcript, apologies.
[08:02] [Speaker 2 / Samir O mislabel?]: uh so, for the warm cache test we should also randomize prefixes to avoid overfitting to a single session.
[08:10] Priya Nair: agreed. randomize but keep semantics.
[08:14] [00:08:30] Priya Nair: We'll also recommend a variant-level gating rule: if TPOT p99 increases by more than 30% vs baseline or quality delta > 5% drop, fail the variant.
[08:29] Samir Patel: And who signs off on success?
[08:32] Jordan Lee: Suggested sign-offs: SkyBridge Product (Maya), SkyBridge SRE (Rajiv), Redwood AE (Jordan) and Redwood SE (Priya). We'll include a sign-off checklist in the report.
[08:43] [00:25:00] Jordan Lee: Recap of concrete items: Redwood sends benchmark harness, measurement plan doc, and security artifacts; SkyBridge shares prompt corpus and provisions VPC sandbox; both sides schedule the first run window.
[08:59] Maya Chen: Can you also share a pricing estimate for the dedicated capacity for the 3-week pilot? we need budget approval.
[09:06] Jordan Lee: Yes we'll include a pilot pricing sheet with reserved hours and burst cost estimates.
[09:12] Rajiv Kapoor: One last question on telemetry retention — how long will Redwood keep the raw traces?
[09:18] Priya Nair: By default we keep aggregated metrics for 90 days; raw traces can be kept per agreement — for the POC we recommend aggregated only unless you request raw traces. We'll include options in the security pack.
[09:28] Samir Patel: ok thanks.
[09:31] Jordan Lee: Great. final check — any blockers?
[09:34] Rajiv Kapoor: no blockers from SRE if we get the IAM details.
[09:37] Elena Marks: none from ML.
[09:38] Jordan Lee: Perfect. we'll follow up with the runbook and schedule. thanks everyone.

Note: timestamps in the auto-transcript are approximate and occasionally mis-attributed. Some speaker labels are generic (Speaker 2) where auto-attribution failed.
